summary: Ezekiel 32 (32 verses) continues the story of glory. Starting with 'In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows glory lived out in chebar canal, babylon. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,
Also in the twelfth year, in the fifteenth day of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,
“For I have put his terror in the land of the living. He will be laid among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, even Pharaoh and all his multitude,” says the Lord Yahweh.

questions.question: What is happening in Ezekiel 32?
questions.answer: In 32 verses, this chapter ezekiel 32 (32 verses) continues the story of glory. starting with 'in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day of the month, yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart. The setting is chebar canal, babylon, written to exiles in babylon. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ezekiel and why 32 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally ezekiel, addressed to exiles in babylon around ~593-571 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as visions, oracles — its themes of glory, idolatry build on what came before.

questions.question: Are there any difficult words here?
questions.answer: Scan for names, places, or repeated abstract words like righteousness, covenant, or glory. The glossary below defines up to 3 that show up most. Ask: who is this person, what does this word mean in everyday terms?

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through glory and idolatry, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 25 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'They have made Elam a bed among the slain with all her multitude. Her graves are around her, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for their terror was caused in the land ...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about glory. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
